narr: In this section, we'll explore the judicial and legal framework of Uzbekistan, focusing on key terms and concepts related to its legal system and human rights developments.
Let's start by examining some important terminology that forms the foundation of Uzbekistan's legal structure.

data.heading: Key Terms
bullets: Military Tribunal: special court of war time with proceedings within 24 hours, no appeal until 1943 — three permanent members
People's Assessors: participated in collegial consideration of cases; summoned from a list for 10 days a year with salary retention
Judicial Chamber: highest judicial instance of Turkestan, created during the reforms of 1897–1899 (Tashkent Judicial Chamber)
CPC (Criminal Procedure Code): first systematized CPC introduced on August 1, 1922; CPC of the Uzbek SSR of 1959 from January 1, 1960
Oliy Majlis: name of the supreme representative body enshrined during work on the Constitution; since the 2000s — a bicameral parliament
Strategy of Actions 2017–2021: program of the fourth stage of legal development; judicial and legal reform as its second priority

narr: Let's break down these key terms that define Uzbekistan's legal landscape.

First, the Military Tribunal served as a special court during wartime, with proceedings required to be completed within 24 hours and no right to appeal until 1943 when it was expanded to three permanent members.

People's Assessors played a crucial role in the judicial process by participating in the collective consideration of cases. They were summoned from a special list for service of 10 days per year while retaining their regular salary.

The Judicial Chamber represented the highest judicial authority in Turkestan, established during the significant legal reforms between 1897 and 1899, with the Tashkent Judicial Chamber being a key implementation.
Regarding the Criminal Procedure Code, Uzbekistan introduced its first systematized version on August 1, 1922, with the Uzbek SSR's CPC coming into effect on January 1, 1960.

The Oliy Majlis, which means 'Supreme Assembly,' is the name given to Uzbekistan's highest representative body, which was formally established during constitutional work and has functioned as a bicameral parliament since the 2000s.
Finally, the Strategy of Actions for 2017–2021 represents the fourth stage of legal development in Uzbekistan, with judicial and legal reform identified as its second priority area.

data.title: Week 6
data.subtitle: Human Rights and Elimination of Forced Labor

narr: Moving to Week 6, we focus on human rights with particular emphasis on the elimination of forced labor in Uzbekistan.

This week addresses critical questions about forced labor according to ILO Conventions No. 29 and No. 105, Uzbekistan's implementation of these international standards, and the systemic issue of child labor in the cotton sector.

data.heading: Week 6 Learning Objectives
bullets: Understanding forced labor according to ILO Conventions No. 29 and No. 105
How Uzbekistan has implemented international labor standards
Institutional mechanisms to combat forced labor formed since 1992
Why child labor became systemic in the cotton sector
Scale, conditions and consequences of child labor
State and international community responses to forced labor

narr: Week 6 answers several important questions about forced labor and human rights in Uzbekistan.
First, we need to understand what constitutes forced labor according to ILO Conventions No. 29 and No. 105, and how Uzbekistan has implemented these international standards.
Second, we'll examine the institutional mechanisms that have been developed since 1992 specifically to combat forced labor.
Third, we'll explore why child labor became systemic in the cotton sector, including its scale, the conditions under which it occurs, and its consequences.
Finally, we'll analyze how both the state of Uzbekistan and the international community have responded to these challenges.

data.heading: Key Provisions: Forced Labor Definition and ILO Conventions
bullets: According to ILO estimates (2017), 40.3 million people are in modern slavery: 24.9 million in forced labor, 15.4 million in forced marriage; every fourth victim is a child
Convention No. 29 (1930) defines forced labor as 'all work or service which is exacted from any person under the threat of any penalty and to which he has not offered himself voluntarily'
The definition is based on four elements: work or service; any person; involuntary nature; threat of penalty
Article 2 of Convention No. 29 excludes military service, ordinary civic obligations, work under court sentence, emergencies, and minor community works
Convention No. 105 (1957) requires immediate abolition of forced labor in five specific cases
Uzbekistan has ratified 17 ILO conventions (including 8 fundamental ones) and 1 protocol as of January 1, 2021

narr: Let's examine the key provisions regarding forced labor, starting with the international definitions and standards.

According to ILO estimates from 2017, a staggering 40.3 million people are trapped in modern slavery worldwide, with 24.9 million in forced labor and 15.4 million in forced marriage. Shockingly, every fourth victim is a child.

Convention No. 29 from 1930 provides the foundational definition of forced labor as 'all work or service which is exacted from any person under the threat of any penalty and to which he has not offered himself voluntarily.'
This definition rests on four essential elements: the nature of the work or service, that it applies to any person, its involuntary character, and the presence of a threat of penalty.

Importantly, Article 2 of Convention No. 29 explicitly excludes certain situations from this definition, including military service, ordinary civic obligations, work under court sentence, emergencies, and minor community works.

Convention No. 105 from 1957 goes further by requiring the immediate abolition of forced labor in five specific cases, including political coercion, labor mobilization for economic development, labor discipline, punishment for strikes, and discrimination.
As of January 1, 2021, Uzbekistan has ratified 17 ILO conventions (including 8 fundamental ones) and 1 protocol, demonstrating its commitment to these international standards.

data.heading: Uzbekistan and International Labor Standards
bullets: Uzbekistan has ratified conventions Nos. 29 and 105, the 2014 Protocol to Convention No. 29 (ratified June 25, 2019, entered into force September 16, 2020)
Also ratified: convention No. 182 on worst forms of child labor and No. 138 on minimum age
The 1966 UN covenants on civil and political rights and on economic, social and cultural rights have been ratified
T. Narbaeva, head of delegation to the 103rd session of the International Labour Conference, emphasized: 'Ratification of conventions is only 50 percent of the solution to the problem'
The remaining 50 percent involves implementation of norms and changing the mindset of farmers and employers

narr: Let's explore Uzbekistan's relationship with international labor standards in more detail.

Uzbekistan has ratified several key conventions, including Nos. 29 and 105, as well as the 2014 Protocol to Convention No. 29, which was ratified on June 25, 2019, and entered into force on September 16, 2020.
Additionally, Uzbekistan has ratified convention No. 182 addressing the worst forms of child labor and No. 138 concerning the minimum age for employment.
The country has also ratified the 1966 UN covenants on civil and political rights and on economic, social and cultural rights, demonstrating comprehensive commitment to human rights standards.

T. Narbaeva, head of Uzbekistan's delegation to the 103rd session of the International Labour Conference, offered an important perspective: 'Ratification of conventions is only 50 percent of the solution to the problem.'
She emphasized that the remaining 50 percent involves the actual implementation of these norms and changing the mindset of farmers and employers who may resist these changes.

data.heading: Prohibition of Forced Labor in National Legislation
bullets: Article 37 of the Constitution prohibits forced labor, except for serving a sentence by court order and other cases provided for by law
Article 10 of the Labor Code allows for the direct application of ratified conventions
Article 7 defines forced labor as 'the performance of work under the threat of any penalty (including as a means of maintaining labor discipline)'
A defect in the national definition: the element of voluntary non-offering of services has been excluded
Due to this exclusion, coercion outside of labor relations may not fall under the norm
Responsibility is established by Art. 1482 of the Criminal Code and Art. 51 of the Administrative Code, but only for 'administrative coercion to labor'

narr: Now let's examine how Uzbekistan's national legislation addresses forced labor.
Article 37 of the Constitution explicitly prohibits forced labor, with exceptions only for serving a sentence by court order and other cases specifically provided for by law.
Article 10 of the Labor Code permits the direct application of ratified international conventions, creating a pathway for international standards to be implemented domestically.
Article 7 defines forced labor as 'the performance of work under the threat of any penalty (including as a means of maintaining labor discipline).'
However, critics note a significant defect in this national definition: the element of voluntary non-offering of services has been excluded from the international standard.
This exclusion means that coercion occurring outside of formal labor relationships may not be adequately covered by this legal norm.

Responsibility for forced labor is established by Article 1482 of the Criminal Code and Article 51 of the Administrative Code, but these provisions currently address only 'administrative coercion to labor,' suggesting a need for broader coverage.

data.heading: Khoshar: Voluntary Labor and Exceptions
bullets: Uzbek legislation uses a single term 'forced labor' (majburiy mehnat)
A special place is occupied by the institution of khoshar: defined as 'voluntary, selfless participation of the majority in completing a task'
The Resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers of May 10, 2018, No. 349 allows for involvement in public works only on a voluntary basis
Public works require the presence of corresponding document of the President or resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers
Greening and improvement works can be organized without strict permission
Coercion to khoshar under the threat of punishment is a direct sign of forced labor

narr: An interesting aspect of Uzbekistan's legal framework is the concept of khoshar, which requires special attention.
Uzbek legislation uses a single term 'forced labor' (majburiy mehnat), but within this framework, khoshar holds a special place.
Khoshar is defined as 'voluntary, selfless participation of the majority in completing a task,' suggesting a cultural practice of collective voluntary work.

The Resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers from May 10, 2018, No. 349 specifies that involvement in public works, including construction and agricultural activities, is only permitted on a voluntary basis.

These public works require the presence of corresponding authorization, either from the President or through a resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers, though greening and improvement works can be organized with less strict permission.
Crucially, any coercion to participate in khoshar under the threat of punishment is considered a direct sign of forced labor, blurring the line between voluntary cultural practice and forced labor.

data.heading: Three Periods of Formation of Institutional Mechanisms
bullets: First period (1992–2007): Uzbekistan joined the ILO, ratified conventions Nos. 29 and 105, adopted the Labor Code and the Employment Law, created state labor inspections
Second period (2008–2016): international organizations reported on systematic use of forced and child labor; ratified conventions Nos. 182 and 138 and the UN protocol on trafficking
Second period continued: adopted the Law 'On Combating Trafficking in Persons' and resolutions Nos. 207, 82, 132
Second period continued: created an interdepartmental commission and a Rehabilitation Center; in 2013 established the Coordinating Council on Child Labor
Third period (since 2017): established criminal liability for forced labor, formed special mechanisms, resumed cooperation with the ILO

narr: The development of institutional mechanisms to combat forced labor in Uzbekistan can be divided into three distinct periods.

The first period from 1992 to 2007 saw Uzbekistan join the ILO, ratify conventions Nos. 29 and 105, adopt the Labor Code and the Employment Law, and establish state labor inspections, though no specialized structures existed yet.

The second period from 2008 to 2016 was marked by international organizations reporting on the systematic use of forced and child labor, leading to additional ratifications including conventions Nos. 182 and 138 on child labor and the UN protocol on trafficking in persons.

During this second period, Uzbekistan also adopted the Law 'On Combating Trafficking in Persons' and several key resolutions, created an interdepartmental commission and a Rehabilitation Center, and in 2013 established the Coordinating Council on Child Labor.

The third period beginning in 2017 has seen the establishment of criminal liability for forced labor, formation of special mechanisms, and the resumption of cooperation with the ILO through various new commissions and bodies.

data.heading: Third Period Developments (2017–2019)
bullets: Parliamentary Commission established (Senate resolution of October 4, 2017, No. SQ-231-III)
Republican interdepartmental commission created (resolution of May 31, 2018, No. 407)
Tripartite commission formed (resolution of July 3, 2019, No. 553)
National Commission and Institute of the National Rapporteur established (decree PF-5775 of July 30, 2019)

narr: Let's examine the specific developments during the third period since 2017 in more detail.
In 2017, a Parliamentary Commission was established through Senate resolution No. SQ-231-III on October 4, indicating the growing legislative attention to these issues.
The following year, on May 31, 2018, a Republican interdepartmental commission was created through resolution No. 407, demonstrating a coordinated governmental approach.
In 2019, a tripartite commission was formed on July 3 through resolution No. 553, suggesting inclusion of government, employer, and worker representatives.

Most significantly, on July 30, 2019, decree PF-5775 established both a National Commission and an Institute of the National Rapporteur, indicating a comprehensive institutional framework for addressing forced labor.

data.heading: Three Types of Mechanisms and National Monitoring
bullets: Three types of mechanisms are currently in operation: collegial bodies, specialized commissions, and monitoring institutions
Collegial bodies include the National Commission on Combating Trafficking in Persons and Forced Labor
Coordination bodies include the Coordinating Council on Child Labor established in 2013
Monitoring mechanisms include the Institute of the National Rapporteur created in 2019
These mechanisms reflect a comprehensive approach to addressing forced labor at multiple levels
The establishment of these institutions demonstrates Uzbekistan's commitment to implementing international standards

narr: Today, Uzbekistan operates three main types of mechanisms to combat forced labor, each serving different functions in the overall system.
First, collegial bodies like the National Commission on Combating Trafficking in Persons and Forced Labor provide high-level coordination and policy development.
Second, coordination bodies such as the Coordinating Council on Child Labor, established in 2013, focus on specific aspects of the problem, particularly child labor.
Third, monitoring mechanisms like the Institute of the National Rapporteur, created in 2019, oversee implementation and report on progress.
Together, these mechanisms reflect a comprehensive approach to addressing forced labor at multiple levels of governance and society.
The establishment of these diverse institutions demonstrates Uzbekistan's growing commitment to implementing international standards and addressing systemic issues of forced labor.
